intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the exercises with a pencil, answer the recall questions without looking, and write your own notes in the margins beside mine.

sections.title: Why WASH matters and what it covers
sections.big_idea: Water, sanitation and hygiene block **one route of infection** at three points, yet India runs them as three programmes.
in_plain_words: Diarrhoea and worm infections travel from one person's faeces to another person's mouth. A toilet keeps faeces out of the environment, safe water keeps them out of the drink and soap keeps them off the hands that feed children. The F-diagram draws the route: faeces, fluids, fingers, flies, fields, food, new host.

Measurement matters as much as the route. Access, use, safety and function are four separate numbers, and most public claims are access claims. **Ask which of the four any figure is**, and look at who is left out of the averages: women who fetch water, and Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe households.

left.title: Primary barriers
items: Pits and tanks emptied and treated

key_terms.meaning: Water, sanitation and hygiene, taught together.
The route faeces take to reach a new mouth.
Stops faeces entering the environment.
Stops existing contamination reaching a mouth.
A service whose benefit reaches neighbours as well as the owner.

worked_example.title: Sort the barriers and the measure
worked_example.setup: Sort four actions into primary or secondary barriers, then read one figure from the NSS 76th round.
steps: A toilet that every member uses stops faeces entering the environment: primary.
Safe emptying of a full pit is also primary.
Handwashing with soap before food acts on contamination already present: secondary.
Treating drinking water at home is secondary. The NSS found 65.3% of households did not treat it.
Households that did treat: 100 − 65.3 = 34.7%.
worked_example.answer: Primary: toilet use and pit emptying. Secondary: handwashing and treatment. 34.7% of households treated water.

mistakes: Reading a national average without asking who is below it. Distance, caste and wealth shape who goes without.
Counting toilets built as if they measured health. Use and what happens afterwards decide that.
Treating the spillover as a family matter. Open defecation raises exposure for every child nearby.

recall.q: What are the four measurements to separate?
recall.a: Access, use, safety and function.

recall.q: Name two primary barriers.
recall.a: A toilet every member uses, and safe emptying of pits and tanks.

recall.q: Why does sanitation behave like a public good?
recall.a: A household's practice changes the exposure of every child nearby.

recall.q: What does the course follow first, the route or the programmes?
recall.a: The route of infection first, and the programmes second.

sections.title: The JMP service ladders
sections.big_idea: The JMP stacks conditions on each rung, so **failing one condition drops a household** and safely managed figures fall far below access.
in_plain_words: The WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme tracks SDG targets 6.1 and 6.2 with one set of definitions. Water has five rungs from surface water to safely managed, sanitation has five from open defecation to safely managed, and hygiene has three. The 30-minute line separates basic from limited water.

The JMP does not run a survey of its own. It fits trend lines through many surveys and records and reads off yearly values. **A smooth line is a fitted value**, so open the country file before quoting a year, and remember that 'improved' describes a technology and says nothing about the water on the day.

diagram.caption: the drinking water ladder, top rung first

key_terms.meaning: The WHO/UNICEF body that tracks SDG 6.1 and 6.2.
A source type that by design can deliver safe water.
The top rung, passing every condition at once.
A handwashing place at home with soap and water.
A yearly estimate read off a trend line.

worked_example.title: Place households on the water ladder
worked_example.setup: Place three households on the drinking water ladder.
steps: Household A uses a protected well one hour away, round trip. It is improved but takes over 30 minutes: limited.
Household B has an improved source within 20 minutes round trip but not on premises: basic.
Household C has a tap in the yard, water when needed, and clean water: safely managed.
Check the gap in India for 2024: 98.1 − 76.4 = 21.7 percentage points between improved and safely managed.
worked_example.answer: A limited, B basic, C safely managed; the India gap is 21.7 points.

mistakes: Treating 'improved' as proof that water is safe. It records the technology at the source.
Quoting the JMP figure for one year without opening the country file.
Reading a safely managed figure as a measured value when it is the minimum of three proportions.
Quoting only the top rung of a ladder because it flatters a programme.

recall.q: Where is the line between basic and limited water?
recall.a: A round trip of 30 minutes including queuing.

recall.q: What does the JMP take for safely managed water?
recall.a: The lowest of three proportions: on premises, available when needed, and free from contamination.

recall.q: How does the JMP measure hygiene?
recall.a: By looking at the handwashing place and whether water and soap are there.

recall.q: What are the five habits for reading a ladder chart?
recall.a: Read top and bottom rung together; people or households; separate rural and urban; find the word estimate; find the oldest input.

sections.title: India's numbers from the JMP, NFHS and NSS
sections.big_idea: The three sources use different units and years. **Always say which survey a figure came from**, and note that NFHS-6 has no sanitation row.
in_plain_words: For 2024 the JMP puts safely managed drinking water at 76.4%, at least basic sanitation at 83.4% and basic hygiene at 89.7%. The safely managed sanitation top rung has no national estimate. Rural and urban differ sharply, and the binding constraint for safely managed water is the tap at home.

NFHS gives round-by-round trends, but the NFHS-6 India fact sheet carries no sanitation indicator. The NSS 76th round of 2018 remains the most detailed national WASH survey, and it showed latrine access still followed household spending. **Any claim of universal coverage has to explain that gap.**

key_terms.meaning: National Family Health Survey, in rounds 4, 5 and 6.
The 2018 survey of 1,06,838 households on water and sanitation.
The lowest of the three criteria, which sets the result.
A fifth of households ranked by consumption.
NFHS measure for women aged 15 to 24.

worked_example.title: Turn percentages into people
worked_example.setup: India's population is about 145 crore (UN figures used by the JMP). The JMP open defecation share is 6.7% in 2024.
steps: People defecating in the open: 145 × 0.067 = 9.7 crore.
Rural latrine access by wealth, 2018: richest fifth 86.7%, poorest fifth 53.5%.
The gap: 86.7 − 53.5 = 33.2 points.
The deck calls this a 33-point gap four years into Swachh Bharat.
worked_example.answer: About 9.7 crore people, and a 33-point wealth gap in rural latrine access in 2018.

mistakes: Citing NFHS-6 for sanitation. Its India fact sheet has no sanitation indicator.
Mixing households and people. JMP and NFHS mostly count people, NSS highlights count households.
Comparing the NFHS-6 menstrual figure with the 77.3% published for NFHS-5 instead of the recomputed 77.6%.
Quoting the sanitation top rung without the caveat that data are insufficient.

recall.q: Which rung of the JMP sanitation ladder cannot be estimated nationally for India?
recall.a: Safely managed, because data on emptied and treated sludge are insufficient.

recall.q: Why is the tap at home the binding constraint for safely managed water?
recall.a: On-premises access at 76.4% is the lowest of the three criteria.

recall.q: What did the NSS 76th round find about rural latrine access by wealth?
recall.a: It rose from 53.5% in the poorest fifth to 86.7% in the richest.

recall.q: What does the missing NFHS-6 row prevent?
recall.a: Setting a district's sanitation figure beside its child outcomes from one sample.

sections.title: What Swachh Bharat Mission built
sections.big_idea: The mission built a great deal, but its numbers **count structures and declarations**. Use was nobody's line item.
in_plain_words: SBM(G) launched on 2 October 2014 with a target of ODF status by 2 October 2019, paid a household incentive and shared costs between Centre and states. Phase II added waste management and ODF Plus labels. SBM(U) built four certifications, from ODF to Water+.

Every headline figure, such as 12 crore latrines, is what states report into the management information system. The record says nothing about use five years later. Surveys show a large fall in open defecation, yet coercion was also reported. **Say both: open defecation fell steeply, and it did not reach zero.**

key_terms.meaning: Open-defecation-free status.
A village sustaining ODF with waste arrangements and cleanliness.
The SBM(G) management information system states report into.
A town safely managing sewage, faecal sludge and septage.
Pressure to build latrines, including withholding benefits.

worked_example.title: Declared versus verified, and cost shares
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a scheme with a cost of 100 crore. The deck gives 60:40 for most states, 90:10 for the north-eastern and Himalayan states and Jammu and Kashmir.
steps: Villages declared ODF Plus (Model): 4,89,526. Verified: 4,15,915.
Centre's share at 60:40: 100 × 0.6 = 60 crore, states 40 crore.
Centre's share at 90:10: 100 × 0.9 = 90 crore, states 10 crore.
worked_example.answer: About 74,000 villages are declared and not yet verified. The Centre pays 60 crore at 60:40 and 90 crore at 90:10.

mistakes: Treating 12 crore toilets as 12 crore toilets in use. The count is of structures.
Reading 'coverage 100%' as universal use. It is households recorded as having a toilet.
Treating a verified village as independently surveyed. Verification stays inside the programme.

recall.q: What is the household incentive under SBM(G)?
recall.a: ₹12,000 for eligible households building an individual latrine.

recall.q: What are the four SBM-U certifications?
recall.a: ODF, ODF+, ODF++ and Water+.

recall.q: What does IMIS record for a latrine?
recall.a: That it was built. It does not record whether it is used or still stands.

recall.q: Which two facts must be said together about open defecation?
recall.a: It fell steeply, and it did not reach zero by October 2019.

sections.title: ODF claims and the survey evidence
sections.big_idea: A declaration, a verification and a measurement are **three different claims**. Explain the gap before choosing a number.
in_plain_words: A declaration is binary for a whole village, a verification is a check inside the government, and a measurement is a sample survey of people with a margin of error. A village at 90% use is not ODF by definition, yet a declaration can still be filed for it.

Surveys also disagree with each other, for five reasons: who answers, question order, unit, who runs it, and season. The NSS printed its own caveat that question order may have inflated latrine access. Owning and using a latrine are separate facts, and caste may explain why some owners avoid a small pit. **Test that argument in your district.**

diagram.root: Three ways to know ODF status
diagram.caption: only the third is a survey estimate

key_terms.meaning: The village or panchayat states no one defecates in the open.
A later check under the programme's own protocol.
A survey estimate of the share of people.
Answers shaped by question order or desire to please.
Two pits used in turn, with a rest period before emptying.

worked_example.title: Size the gaps between sources
worked_example.setup: Use the comparison table for rural India.
steps: Programme records report 100% coverage in October 2019; the NSS 76th round found 71.3% latrine access in 2018. Gap: 100 − 71.3 = 28.7 points.
Rural open defecation fell in the JMP estimate from 44.4% (2014) to 10.7% (2024): 44.4 − 10.7 = 33.7 points.
NFHS-5 gave 25.5% and HCES 18.0%. The two points differ by 25.5 − 18.0 = 7.5 points.
Explain each gap through the five reasons before picking one figure.
worked_example.answer: 28.7, 33.7 and 7.5 points. Each gap needs a reason before a number is chosen.

mistakes: Quoting a declaration as if it were a survey estimate.
Asking about scheme benefits before asking about the latrine, which the NSS warned could inflate the answer.
Asking one respondent to speak for the whole household.
Assuming that owning a latrine means every member uses it.

recall.q: What are the five reasons two surveys of one year differ?
recall.a: Who answers, question order, unit, who runs it, and timing and season.

recall.q: What did the NSS warn about its own latrine figure?
recall.a: Benefit questions were asked first, so respondent bias may have affected reported access.

recall.q: What share of rural latrine households' members never used it in 2018?
recall.a: 3.5% in the NSS 76th round.

recall.q: What does the caste argument predict about pit latrines?
recall.a: Use is lower where latrines are small pits, because emptying is linked to work assigned by caste.

sections.title: Jal Jeevan Mission, from taps to working water
sections.big_idea: A tap connection is counted once. **Water has to arrive every day, in quantity and of quality**, and only a third-party assessment shows that.
in_plain_words: Jal Jeevan Mission promises a functional household tap connection to every rural household, with at least 55 litres per person per day, to the BIS:10500 standard. Connections grew about five-fold in six years, but the management system records pipes installed and says nothing about litres delivered.

The 2022 functionality assessment tested quantity, regularity and quality. A connection is fully functional only if all three hold. Supply patterns, lab capacity and village committees all fell short. **Ask for days of supply, hours per day and who runs O&M**, in dry and wet seasons.

diagram.caption: only the last step checks the water

key_terms.meaning: Functional Household Tap Connection.
Litres per capita per day; the standard is 55.
All households in a unit have tap water supply.
Village water and sanitation committee, also called Pani Samiti.
Operation and maintenance after construction.

worked_example.title: Classify a tap connection
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a connection delivers 50 litres per person per day, runs daily for 12 months and the water is potable. The deck's rules: quantity 55 or more is full, over 40 to under 55 is partial.
steps: Quantity: 50 lpcd falls between 40 and 55, so partially functional.
Regularity: daily for 12 months, so fully functional on this criterion.
Quality: potable, so fully functional on this criterion.
A connection is fully functional only if all three hold, so the weakest criterion decides.
Check the supply breakdown: 4% + 14% + 8% = 26% of households without daily supply.
worked_example.answer: The connection is partially functional. 26% of households lacked daily supply in 2022.

mistakes: Quoting the connection count as the share of households with working water.
Ignoring lab limits. Labs reported on 83% of samples and took over 48 hours.
Assuming a village committee runs the scheme. Only 14% were responsible for O&M in 2022.
Doing one visit in one season for a service that varies by month.

recall.q: What is the quantity standard for a fully functional tap?
recall.a: 55 litres per capita per day or more.

recall.q: Which stage of the IMIS ladder checks quantity, regularity and quality?
recall.a: The functional stage, via a third-party assessment.

recall.q: What share of households received water on all seven days in 2022?
What did the assessment recommend first about village committees?
recall.a: Scale up VWSC participation in O&M.

sections.title: Groundwater depletion and contamination
sections.big_idea: The national extraction figure hides local failure. **Check your block's category** and its quality record before you design a scheme.
in_plain_words: The stage of extraction is annual extraction divided by the extractable resource. For India as a whole it is 60.63%. Blocks fall into safe, semi-critical, critical and over-exploited categories, and regulation tightens with each. A block average can also hide a cluster of failing borewells.

Quality needs separate attention. Nitrate, fluoride, arsenic and uranium exceed limits in some samples, and arsenic and fluoride cause harm through years of drinking. Responses range from piped supply to deep wells and interim plants. **Count recharge only if the structure fills and is maintained.**

diagram.note: safe below 70%, semi-critical 70 to 90%, critical 90 to 100%, over-exploited above 100%

key_terms.meaning: Billion cubic metres.
Annual extraction as a share of the extractable resource.
An assessment unit extracting more than 100% of its resource.
The national aquifer mapping programme.
A scheme for community groundwater management in 80 districts.

worked_example.title: Work the extraction numbers
worked_example.setup: Use the 2025 account. Annual extraction is 247.22 BCM and the extractable resource is 407.75 BCM. Of 6,762 assessment units, 730 are over-exploited.
steps: Stage of extraction: 247.22 ÷ 407.75 = 60.63%.
Share of units over-exploited: 730 ÷ 6,762 = 10.80%.
A block at 85% sits in the semi-critical band of 70 to 90%.
A block at 105% is over-exploited and faces the highest charges and no new large-scale industries.
worked_example.answer: 60.63% nationally, 10.80% of units over-exploited, and block categories follow the bands.

mistakes: Using the national 60.63% as if it described every block.
Reading 'isolated pockets' as reassurance when one sample in five exceeds the nitrate limit.
Counting a quality-affected habitation as safe because a treatment plant was installed.
Building a piped scheme on a borewell in an over-exploited block with no fallback.

recall.q: How is the stage of extraction calculated?
recall.a: Annual extraction divided by the extractable resource.

recall.q: How many assessment units were over-exploited in 2025?
Which contaminants does the deck link to years of drinking?
recall.a: Arsenic and fluoride, which occur naturally in some aquifers.

recall.q: Where do you look up a block's category?
recall.a: The CGWB National Compilation of Dynamic Ground Water Resources, 2025.

sections.title: Who governs water and sanitation
sections.big_idea: Water is a State subject, and the Centre pays and advises. **Find out who signs the work order** before you assign blame or ask for action.
in_plain_words: States build and often run schemes, choose technology and set tariffs. The Centre designs centrally sponsored schemes, sets guidelines and runs the CGWB and CGWA. Local government comes in through the 73rd and 74th Amendments, but devolution under the word 'may' depends on each state.

Pollution law, institutions and money each have a place. The Water Act, 1974 regulates discharge but gives no one a supply entitlement. Construction is funded centrally, and operation and maintenance usually is not. **Map the offices for your district before the first field visit.**

diagram.caption: who does what, from the top

key_terms.meaning: A matter primarily the responsibility of State governments.
Gave panchayats constitutional status from 24 April 1993.
Functions states may give urban local bodies.
Drawing on other schemes' funds for WASH works.
A pollution board condition on a discharger.

worked_example.title: Whom do you ask?
worked_example.setup: Match four problems to the office from the institutions table.
steps: A drain discharges sewage into a village pond: the state pollution control board, under the Water Act, 1974.
A city says it licenses desludging trucks but keeps no trip record: the urban local body's desludging records.
A borewell scheme sits in an over-exploited block: the CGWB for the block category.
A village needs its water accounts: the gram panchayat or VWSC.
Check a money rule: 60,816 × 0.02 = 1,216.32 crore, the most Uttar Pradesh could use for water quality surveillance from its central allocation.
worked_example.answer: Pollution board, urban local body, CGWB, gram panchayat. Up to 1,216.32 crore for quality surveillance in Uttar Pradesh.

mistakes: Accepting 'it is the Centre's problem' or 'it is the state's' without finding who signs the work order.
Reading the Water Act, 1974 as a right to water. Entitlements come from scheme guidelines.
Looking for money for operation and maintenance in central scheme lines that fund construction.
Expecting devolution to be uniform when each state decides what to hand down.

recall.q: Whose responsibility is water, primarily?
recall.a: State governments, with the Centre supporting through schemes.

recall.q: What did the 2022 assessment find about VWSCs in charge of O&M?
recall.a: They were in charge in 14% of villages.

recall.q: What does the Water Act, 1974 not do?
recall.a: It does not guarantee anyone a supply of water.

recall.q: What share of households had their complaint resolved in 2022?

sections.title: Faecal sludge, sanitation work and the 2013 Act
sections.big_idea: A toilet is the start of a chain. **Safe sanitation includes emptying, transport and treatment**, and the people who do it need protection.
in_plain_words: Most Indian toilets with access are not on a sewer: half use septic tanks and more than a fifth use pits. Every pit and tank fills. The service chain runs from containment through emptying, transport and treatment to disposal, and it often breaks at the middle links.

The 2013 Act bans manual scavenging and hazardous cleaning of sewers and septic tanks, yet 317 sanitation workers died in 2021 to 2025 by the Ministry's figure. NAMASTE mechanises the work and registers the workers. **Caste is part of the design brief**, since the person who empties the pit is chosen by the design.

key_terms.meaning: Containment, emptying, transport, treatment, disposal or reuse.
Faecal sludge treatment plant.
Banned work of handling human excreta by hand.
A scheme for mechanised sanitation and worker registration.
Sewer and septic tank worker.

worked_example.title: Read the sewer and septic numbers
worked_example.setup: Use the 2018 latrine type table for all households with access: sewer 17.0%, septic tank 50.1%, twin or single pit 22.5%.
steps: Households on sewer or septic tank: 17.0 + 50.1 = 67.1%.
Households on pits of either kind: 22.5%.
Every septic tank and pit fills, so most of these 67.1% and 22.5% depend on emptying services.
The deck's NAMASTE figures: 89,248 profiled and 75,710 covered. 89,248 − 75,710 = 13,538 profiled workers without cover.
worked_example.answer: 67.1% on sewers or septic tanks, 22.5% on pits, and 13,538 profiled workers not yet covered.

mistakes: Counting toilets as safe sanitation when nobody tracks where sludge goes.
Quoting the 58,098 figure as the number of manual scavengers. It is a floor.
Merging the 58,098 identified manual scavengers with the 89,248 profiled workers. They are different groups.
Leaving out the date and source on figures about deaths.

recall.q: What are the five links of the service chain?
recall.a: Containment, emptying, transport, treatment, and disposal or reuse.

recall.q: Which pit design avoids handling fresh excreta?
recall.a: The twin leach pit, emptied after a rest period of one and a half years.

recall.q: When did the 2013 Act come into force?
recall.a: 6 December 2013.

recall.q: What is the cash assistance paid to each identified family?
recall.a: ₹40,000 one-time.

sections.title: Handwashing and menstrual health
sections.big_idea: Soap works when people use it. **Reported handwashing runs far above observed handwashing**, and large household WASH trials found little effect on growth.
in_plain_words: Pooled studies estimated that washing hands with soap could cut diarrhoea risk by 42 to 47%, and the Karachi trial found large effects of plain soap. But NSS reports of soap use are much higher than what observers saw in the SuperAmma villages, where baseline handwashing was close to zero.

Large trials in Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Bangladesh, Kenya and Zimbabwe found small or no effects on child growth, for reasons of low coverage, elementary interventions and fading adherence. Menstrual health needs water, privacy and disposal too. **Read a null result carefully.**

key_terms.meaning: After defecation, after cleaning a child, before cooking and before eating.
An observer records behaviour at key events.
How long households keep using what they were given.
A trial that finds no measurable effect.
Menstrual products counted as hygienic in NFHS.

worked_example.title: Compare two menstrual health figures
worked_example.setup: NFHS-6 reports 79.2% of women aged 15 to 24 using hygienic menstrual protection. NFHS-5 published 77.3% and NFHS-6 recomputed it as 77.6%.
steps: Wrong comparison: 79.2 − 77.3 = 1.9 points.
Right comparison on the same basis: 79.2 − 77.6 = 1.6 points.
The deck says the right rise is under two points.
Also note SuperAmma at six months: 37 − 6 = 31 points above control villages.
worked_example.answer: 1.6 points on the matching basis; the SuperAmma effect at six months was 31 points above controls.

mistakes: Reporting handwashing from a questionnaire alone.
Concluding from the trials that safe water and sanitation have no health value.
Comparing NFHS-6 with the unrevised NFHS-5 figure.
Promoting menstrual products with no plan for disposal.

recall.q: What did Karachi find about plain soap and antibacterial soap?
recall.a: Plain soap did as well as antibacterial soap.

recall.q: Why was SuperAmma's twelve-month result hard to read?
recall.a: Control villages received a shortened version before then, and both groups stood at 29%.

recall.q: Name two reasons the large trials found little effect.
recall.a: Coverage too low, interventions too elementary, or fading adherence.

recall.q: What does the JMP file say about menstrual health indicators for India?
recall.a: Every column is empty.

sections.title: Climate, drought and water security
sections.big_idea: Scarcity is already in household data. **Source sustainability** is the climate measure a drinking water programme controls directly.
in_plain_words: The NSS found 12.4% of rural households without enough drinking water from the principal source all year in 2018, and the 2022 assessment found 43% of tap households had faced a shortage in piped supply. A dry-season visit and a post-monsoon visit can give different answers about the same village.

Irrigation pumping, weak monsoons, heat and contamination all reach drinking water. Floods, droughts and heat change how toilets behave. The checklist converts evidence into questions for a plan: groundwater category, May yield, flood history, summer supply and quality tests. **Ask each question for both seasons.**

key_terms.meaning: Whether the source will still deliver in a dry year.
A forecast from assumptions, such as the 2030 water gap.
A work that returns water to the aquifer.
How high a toilet base sits above flood level.
An assessment unit classed as saline by CGWB.

worked_example.title: Turn survey shares into a plan
worked_example.setup: NSS 76th round: 87.6% of rural households had sufficient drinking water from the principal source throughout the year.
steps: Share without enough water: 100 − 87.6 = 12.4%.
The 2022 JJM assessment found 43% of tap households had a shortage at some point.
Only 40% of those households had any way to cope.
Plan fieldwork in May and in October so that both seasons appear.
worked_example.answer: 12.4% of rural households lacked sufficient water, and the later survey found a much larger share with some shortage.

mistakes: Treating the doubling of demand by 2030 as a measurement. It is a NITI Aayog projection from 2008 estimates.
Assessing a scheme in one season only.
Building a borewell scheme without a yield test in May.
Siting pits close to shallow wells and drinking sources.

recall.q: What does the deck call the climate adaptation measure a drinking water programme controls?
recall.a: Source sustainability.

recall.q: What happens to a pour-flush toilet in drought?
recall.a: Households ration water for drinking first, and toilet use can fall.

recall.q: What did the CWMI project for 2030?
recall.a: Demand exceeding supply by a factor of two, as a projection.

recall.q: What should a team check before investing in a flood-prone area?
recall.a: Flood history, plinth height and the distance from pits to wells.

sections.title: Monitoring a WASH programme
sections.big_idea: Monitor **use and function** along with construction. Choose few indicators, fix their definitions and triangulate sources.
in_plain_words: There are four kinds of WASH data: programme MIS, government-commissioned surveys, national statistical surveys, and independent studies. Each has a typical error. Use the MIS to find where things were built, a statistical survey to find how many use them, and a small independent check to understand why.

Indicators should match the ladders, such as days of supply last week, litres per person per day and toilet use by each member. Combine self-report, spot checks and observation, and report the gap between them. **Every report should name source, date, unit and collector.**

key_terms.meaning: Management information records of what was built.
Compare several data sources on one question.
Looking for signs such as a wet pan or soap at the handwashing place.
A quick tap-level check that supply has been treated.
The same villages and households followed over rounds.

worked_example.title: Measure litres per person per day
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a household of 5 receives 300 litres at the tap in a day. The standard is 55.
steps: Per person: 300 ÷ 5 = 60 litres per day.
Compare with the standard: 60 − 55 = 5 litres above it.
Repeat in May and in October with bucket and timer.
Record days of supply last week, from 0 to 7.
worked_example.answer: 60 litres per person per day, 5 litres above the standard on the day measured.

mistakes: Reporting handwashing or toilet use from a questionnaire alone.
Changing indicator definitions between rounds, so change is not comparable.
Treating a bacteriological test as a description of the moment sampled and nothing more.
Publishing MIS figures without the survey figures beside them.

recall.q: What are the four kinds of WASH data?
recall.a: Programme MIS, government-commissioned surveys, national statistical surveys, and independent studies and trials.

recall.q: Which parameters were measured on site in the 2022 JJM assessment?
recall.a: pH and residual chlorine.

recall.q: How should toilet use be asked?
recall.a: About the last defecation of each person over two, privately, with child faeces disposal.

recall.q: What four facts should every report name?
recall.a: Data source, date, unit and who collected it.

notes.2: Skim the twelve sections and mark the one closest to your work. The course moves from definitions and ladders to India's numbers, then to the two big missions, groundwater, governance, sludge, hygiene, climate and monitoring. **Sections 2, 3 and 5 give you the habits** the later sections reuse.
notes.4: Learn the three services as three blocks on one route of infection. Toilets keep faeces out of the environment, safe water keeps them out of the drink, and soap keeps them off hands. In India the three sit in **different programmes**, so a district officer sees three dashboards for one problem.
notes.5: Read these three figures as a model of what full coverage could avert. The authors use the SDG ladders as the yardstick, so a household counts as exposed until it reaches safely managed water and sanitation and basic hygiene. **Treat them as estimates**, and cite the Lancet paper when you quote them.
notes.6: Trace the F-diagram from left to right: faeces, fluids, fingers, flies, fields, food, new host. Then sort every intervention into one of two types. **Primary barriers keep faeces out of the environment.** Secondary barriers stop what is already there from reaching a mouth. Handwashing and safe storage are secondary.
notes.7: Sanitation behaves like a public good because your neighbour's practice affects your child. The district evidence shows an association, and the authors say the design is ecological. Take the programme lesson: **count the share of people using toilets**, since a toilet in every house measures only construction.
notes.8: Memorise the four measurements: access, use, safety and function. Most public WASH claims in India are access claims, because a construction programme can count access. The numbers that decide whether children get sick are the harder three. **Ask which of the four any single figure is.**
notes.9: Look at who is missing from the averages. A woman or girl usually walks to fetch water when the tap is not at home. Rural SC and ST households had lower latrine access than the 71.3% rural average, and access rose steeply across wealth quintiles. **Break every national number down by group.**
notes.10: The course map lists eleven steps, and its numbers run one behind the section dividers, so read it as an order of topics and use the dividers for section numbers. The outcomes list is a self-test: if you can do all six, you have **understood the course**.
notes.12: Treat the JMP as the referee for SDG 6.1 and 6.2. It uses one set of definitions so countries and years can be compared. The key idea sits in the last sentence: each top-rung definition stacks conditions, so **one failed condition drops the household**. That is why safely managed figures sit well below access figures.
notes.13: Learn the water ladder from the bottom: surface water, unimproved, limited, basic, safely managed. The 30-minute line separates basic from limited, and it counts the round trip with queuing. A protected well an hour away is **improved but still only limited**. Remember that the line rests on what the respondent estimates.
notes.14: Compare the sanitation ladder with the water ladder. Shared facilities fall to limited, and the top rung depends on what happens after the pit fills. For India the JMP lacks data on sludge emptied and treated, so **the top rung cannot be estimated nationally**. Quote at least basic, or say why you quote the top rung.
notes.15: The hygiene ladder measures the handwashing place: soap and water present gives basic, one missing gives limited. A facility makes washing possible but does not show that anyone washes at the right moments. The menstrual health columns in the JMP file are **empty for India**, which is a gap in national evidence.
notes.16: Remember that the JMP runs no survey of its own. It fits trend lines through many surveys and records and reads off a value for each year. For safely managed water it takes the lowest of three proportions. **Open the country file before quoting a single year**, and look for values in square brackets.
notes.17: Improved describes the technology at the source. It does not tell you whether the water tested clean, whether the tubewell runs dry in May or whether the pit overflows. Work through the two-household example. The final gap, 98.1% improved against 76.4% safely managed, is **21.7 points of difference** between a source and a service.
notes.18: Use the five habits as a checklist whenever you read a ladder chart. In the worked example, the 2024 figure is a fitted value one year past the newest survey points. It may prove right, and it is a projection. The last line is the rule to keep: **quote the full ladder**.
notes.20: Read the table by columns. Water has a safely managed top rung at 76.4%, hygiene is 89.7% basic, and sanitation is the column with a caveat. The country file computes 62.8% safely managed from assumptions while also saying data are insufficient. **Quote 83.4% at least basic, or add the caveat.**
notes.21: Use this chart to see the shape of two decades. Water access was high and rising before either mission began. Sanitation shows the larger movement, with open defecation falling steadily through the Swachh Bharat years. Remember that the line is **a fitted value** and that section 5 explains why survey points under it disagree.
notes.22: Compare rural and urban column by column. Urban wins on safely managed water and on basic hygiene, while rural India has more on-site pits and tanks and less sewer connection. Note the water quality row: **11.9% of rural people using improved sources lack contamination-free water**, a hidden weakness in the access figure.
notes.23: The JMP takes the lowest of three criteria, so the binding constraint decides the safely managed figure. For India that is on-premises access at 76.4%. The practical consequence is that **a working Jal Jeevan Mission tap adds directly** to SDG 6.1. Also note that the quality figure rests on far fewer tests.
notes.24: Read this table across rounds and watch for the blank cells. Improved drinking water rose from 89.9% to 96.5%, while diarrhoea in under-fives moved from 9.2% to 7.3% and then to 7.9%. The rise is small and the survey asks about two weeks, so **season of fieldwork matters**.
notes.25: Remember that the NFHS-6 India fact sheet carries no sanitation indicator at all, though NFHS-5 did. That removes the only national survey that measured sanitation in the same households as child height, anaemia and diarrhoea. **If a report cites NFHS-6 for sanitation, ask which survey the figure came from.**
notes.26: Treat the NSS 76th round as the most detailed national WASH survey and read its rural and urban columns together. It covered 1,06,838 households from July to December 2018. Look at the gap between 94.5% using an improved source and 51.4% with an improved source on premises and sufficient all year. **Layered questions give layered answers.**
notes.27: Look at the quintile chart first, then the slide's closing challenge. A 33-point gap separated the poorest and richest rural fifths four years into Swachh Bharat. **Any later claim of universal coverage has to explain** how the poorest rural households closed it in the final year.
notes.29: Note the design before the results: the aim, the 2 October 2019 target, the household incentive and the cost sharing. Then read the slide's last sentence, which is the thesis of the whole section. **A subsidy paid on construction gives every official a reason to report construction**, and use is nobody's line item.
notes.30: Treat these headline numbers as counts of structures reported by states into IMIS. A latrine is entered when it is built, and the record says nothing about use five years later. The repair campaign shows another side: a campaign that repairs toilets is **also evidence that many need repair**.
notes.31: Read ODF Plus (Model) as a village standard with four parts: sustained ODF status, solid and liquid waste arrangements, visual cleanliness and IEC messages. The table separates declared from verified villages, about 74,000 apart. Remember that **both are recorded in the same programme system** and neither is a household survey.
notes.32: Memorise the four certifications as a ladder: ODF, ODF+, ODF++ and Water+. Each adds a duty, and the last two are the ones that cover sludge and used water. ODF++ is the certification that checks **what happens to the sewage** after it leaves the toilet. Use the timeline to date a claim.
notes.33: Read the official sentence slowly. It reports village declarations and a coverage figure from the programme's own records, so coverage means households recorded as having a toilet. That is an **access measure**. The slide's closing line is the stance to take: a good-faith claim about records is still a claim about records.
notes.34: Treat this slide as one study's report of how targets were enforced. The survey revisited rural households in four states and the paper reports coercion, including threats to withhold benefits. Note the multipliers for Dalit and Scheduled Tribe households. Remember the authors' request: **an evidence-based public discussion** of costs and results.
notes.35: Hold two true statements at once. Every source shows a large fall in open defecation after 2014, and the fall did not reach zero by October 2019. The JMP trend falls at the same pace before and after 2014, so **read the survey points directly**. A report giving only one statement has chosen a side.
notes.37: Use these three verbs as a vocabulary test. Declared means the village says so. Verified means a later check inside the government that runs the programme. Measured means a sample survey estimating a share with a margin of error. A village at 90% use is **not ODF by definition** yet a declaration can still be filed.
notes.38: Read down the figures for rural sanitation and rural open defecation, from 100% in programme records to 10.7% in the JMP estimate. Note the rows measure different things, with access in some and open defecation in others. The slide states its own conclusion: **no survey here supports universal toilet use in 2019**.
notes.39: Look for the amber bars: the NARSS series reports 6.8% in 2019 and 0.8% in 2020, while NFHS-5 and the NSS 78th round report 25.5% and 20.7%. The JMP used all of them, so its fitted line runs between. **A smooth line hides a wide scatter of inputs**, so look at the points.
notes.40: Use the five reasons as a diagnostic when two surveys disagree: who answers, question order, unit, who runs it, and season. Each has a check to run. The summary rule is the practical lesson: **explain the gap before choosing a number**. The deep dive study on asking about each member is worth reading in the source.
notes.41: Read the statistical office's own caveat beside its headline number. Households were asked about scheme benefits before asking about latrine access, which may inflate reported access. For your own questionnaire, **put use and facility questions before benefits** and ask to see the latrine. Even so, the slide says 71.3% is well short of 100%.
notes.42: Compare the two findings on use among owners: 3.5% of rural household members never used the latrine in the national NSS, while 23% of owners over two defecated in the open in four states. The populations and the questions differ. **Both agree that some owners do not use their latrines** and disagree about how many.
notes.43: Treat the caste argument as a hypothesis with a predicted pattern. Coffey and Spears propose that avoidance of pit emptying, an occupation assigned by caste, makes small pits unattractive. Programme responses follow from that: twin pits, visible mechanised emptying and no caste-assigned workers. **Test it in your district** with questions on pit size, fear of filling and who empties.
notes.44: Use the seven questions on any ODF claim, in order. The practical advice is the district exercise: visit a random sample of hamlets at dawn, ask each member where they went yesterday and record the state of each latrine. That week of work is worth **more than any declaration**.
notes.46: Remember JJM's promise in its own terms: a functional household tap connection, with at least 55 litres per capita per day and water meeting the BIS:10500 standard. Har Ghar Jal on the dashboard means all households in a unit are connected. **Both dashboard terms describe connections**, and the service standard sits beside them.
notes.47: Read the chart as administrative counts of connections from JJM-IMIS. Tap connections grew about five-fold in six years. The Budget Speech and the December 2025 review use different bases, 15 crore households and 81.47%. **State which source and date you use** when you quote a connection figure.
notes.48: Follow the five stages from sanction to functional, and notice who reports at each. IMIS records a connection when the pipe and tap are installed. Only the third-party assessment shows quantity, regularity and quality on the day. The mission itself describes 2025 as **a shift from infrastructure to service delivery**.
notes.49: Learn the three criteria that define a fully functional connection: 55 litres or more per person per day, daily supply for 12 months, and potable water. All three must hold at once. The slide credits the assessment for publishing a strict standard, and the sample design (13,303 villages) gives the results weight.
notes.50: Read the fully functional share as the strictest cut: connections that pass quantity, regularity and quality together. In Har Ghar Jal villages 91% of connections worked and 69% were fully functional. Aspirational districts did worse. **Working is not the same as fully functional**, so quote the stricter figure when you describe service.
notes.51: Look at the supply pattern behind the average: 74% of households got water all seven days, for an average of three hours. The health point is on the slide: pipes that empty between supply hours can draw in contamination, so intermittent supply turns a piped system **back into a storage problem**. Monitor days and hours, in dry and wet seasons.
notes.52: Notice that testing is a bottleneck. Labs could report on 83% of samples, tested 30 to 40 a day with a turnaround over 48 hours, and only about a quarter of households had residual chlorine within limits. By December 2025 the system listed 2,863 labs. **Capacity numbers do not show results**, so check what was tested.
notes.53: Read the table as a measure of local institutions. Only 38% of villages had formed a VWSC, 14% had it responsible for O&M, and 3% of households saw a complaint resolved. The assessment's first recommendation was to scale up VWSC participation. **Ask who runs the scheme after the contractor leaves.**
notes.55: Start from the national account and work the division yourself. Annual extraction of 247.22 BCM over an extractable resource of 407.75 BCM gives the stage of extraction of 60.63%. Drinking water competes with farming for one stock, since **hand pumps and piped borewell schemes share the aquifer**.
notes.56: Read the chart as a count of assessment units by category: 730 over-exploited, 201 critical, 758 semi-critical, 4,946 safe and 127 saline. The national 60.63% hides them. These are **the places where drinking water sources fail first**. Look up your own block and skip the national average.
notes.57: Hold two ideas together. Irrigation drives extraction, with NITI Aayog reporting that groundwater is 62% of irrigation water. And averages hide sinks: a block is assessed as a whole. Learn the four categories by stage of extraction (below 70%, 70 to 90%, 90 to 100%, above 100%) and what regulation each triggers.
notes.58: Read the percentages as shares of samples, which are not shares of people. Nitrate above the limit appears in 19.8% of samples, fluoride in 9.04% and arsenic in 3.1%. The government's phrase 'isolated pockets' needs scrutiny: a nitrate exceedance in one sample in five is **a finding about many places at once**.
notes.59: Use the table as a menu of responses and test each for failure. Arsenic and fluoride occur naturally and harm through years of drinking, so households keep using familiar handpumps. The last line is the field rule: an interim plant needs electricity, chemicals and an operator, so **check it runs before you count the habitation safe**.
notes.60: Sort the programmes by what they do: community management (Atal Bhujal), mapping and planning (NAQUIM), and campaigns (Jal Shakti Abhiyan, Amrit Sarovar). Then apply the slide's warning. **Recharge counted as structures has the same weakness as toilets counted as structures**, so ask whether it fills and who maintains it.
notes.61: Use the table as a pre-design checklist for any block. Look up block category, contaminants, the aquifer plan, quality-affected habitations and seasonal water levels. The closing sentence is the stake: a project in an over-exploited block that plans no recharge or alternative source is **planning for its own failure**.
notes.63: Memorise the Ministry's repeated sentence: water is a State subject, and the Centre supports with technical and financial assistance. States build and run schemes and choose technology and tariffs. The practical rule is the last line: when each side blames the other, **find out who signs the work order**.
notes.64: Panchayats and municipalities get their place from the 73rd and 74th Amendments. The 73rd came into force on 24 April 1993 and lists 29 subjects, but the key word is 'may', since each state decides what to devolve. The 14% of villages with VWSCs in charge of O&M shows **how far devolution had reached**.
notes.65: The Water Act, 1974 created the pollution control boards and, with the Environment Act, is the main law against untreated discharge. It protects the sources that drinking schemes draw on, and its consent conditions are public documents. The limit is stated plainly: it regulates pollution and **gives no one a right to a water supply**.
notes.66: Use this table as a contact sheet. Each institution has a role and something you can ask it for. The last sentence tells you why: **most WASH failures fall between two of these offices**. Map them for your district before the first field visit, and note the NCSK and the Ministry of Social Justice for sanitation work.
notes.67: Follow the money in two parts. Cost sharing differs by state group, and convergence draws funds from other programmes. Then use the closing line as the diagnosis: construction is funded centrally while operation and maintenance usually is not, and **that is where schemes fail**. The three questions tell you where records exist.
notes.68: List the channels that exist and compare with how households use them: 71% aware of a grievance mechanism, 5% complaining, 3% resolved. The slide's judgement is blunt. A channel that resolves three households in a hundred is not carrying the load, so **ask for feedback at the tap on a fixed day**.
notes.70: Read the table by where excreta goes. Only 17.0% of households with access used a toilet connected to a sewer in 2018, half used septic tanks, and more than a fifth used pits. Every pit and tank fills, so safety depends on **emptying, transport and treatment** that most towns and villages lacked.
notes.71: Learn the five links in the service chain: containment, emptying, transport, treatment, disposal or reuse. Then look for where it breaks, such as tanks with no soak pit or unregistered trucks. The sentence to keep: **ODF counts toilets, safe sanitation counts the whole chain**. A town can be the first and not the second.
notes.72: Compare the three designs by what they ask of people. Twin pits rest, and the filled pit can be emptied after a rest period of one and a half years. Single pits need desludging at once, with fresh contents. The conclusion is a design rule: **a programme building single pits builds future hazardous work**.
notes.73: Look at urban FSM through plant counts and then ask the town-level questions: is the plant running, how many trucks arrived, are operators licensed and paid. A plant with no trucks treats nothing. ODF++ is the certification that **measures the chain**. Rural sludge management is at an early stage.
notes.74: The 2013 Act bans manual scavenging and hazardous cleaning of sewers and septic tanks, and requires rehabilitation. Read the 58,098 figure correctly: it counts people the 2013 and 2018 surveys found and accepted. People the surveys missed are not in it, so **treat it as a floor**.
notes.75: Report this figure with its source and date: 317 deaths in 2021 to 2025, as reported to the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis. Unreported deaths are not in it. The Act already bans the work, so each death records a failure of enforcement. Ask **who hired the worker** and who decided to send a person into the tank.
notes.76: NAMASTE pairs mechanisation with registration. Read the table as a pipeline: profile workers, cover them with health schemes, provide PPE and emergency units, and subsidise machinery. The footnote matters: the 89,248 profiled workers in hazardous cleaning are **a different group** from the 58,098 manual scavengers identified earlier.
notes.77: Turn the six actions into design rules for your own programme. Build toilets that never need manual emptying of fresh sludge, map who empties and how, write mechanised emptying into contracts and keep emergency numbers. The closing point is moral and practical: **a programme that ignores who will empty the pit has chosen by default**.
notes.79: Keep the evidence in two layers. The review estimates a 42 to 47% drop in diarrhoea risk from handwashing with soap, with warnings on study quality and publication bias. The Karachi trial found large effects of plain soap. The final line sets the programme problem: **the hard part is getting people to wash at the right moments**, every day.
notes.80: Read the chart as what households report. Most say they wash with soap after defecation, and before meals 60.4% used water only. The NSS counted a household as following a practice if most members usually did. Those are reports, and the next slide shows **what observers see**.
notes.81: Compare this chart with the last. Observers watched handwashing at four key events and found it far lower than households report. They told households the study was about domestic water use to reduce bias. The asterisk matters: control villages received a shortened intervention before the 12-month round. **Reported and observed handwashing differ.**
notes.82: SuperAmma tested a campaign built on emotional drivers instead of disease knowledge. Handwashing with soap at key events rose from 1% to 37% at six months against 6% in control villages. At twelve months both groups stood at 29% after controls got a shortened version. **Budget for structured observation** if you report handwashing.
notes.83: Read the trials as a set: five settings, different deliveries, and mostly small effects on growth. Diarrhoea fell in some Bangladesh arms, and Kenya's arms did not reduce it. In Odisha, coverage rose from 9% to 63% with no effect on diarrhoea. **Look at adherence and coverage** in each row before you generalise.
notes.84: Learn three explanations for the null results: coverage too low, interventions too elementary and adherence that fades. Then read the final paragraph, which protects against overreading. The trials show that small household packages do not change growth. They do **not show that community-wide safe water and sanitation lack health value**.
notes.85: Compare NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 on the same basis. NFHS-6 counts reusable and disposable pads, tampons and cups as hygienic, and recomputed NFHS-5 to 77.6%. So the rise is under two points: **compare 79.2% with 77.6%, and leave 77.3% aside**. Always check that a comparison uses a matching basis.
notes.86: Treat menstrual health as a water, privacy and disposal problem as well as a product problem. India has no national JMP estimate on these indicators. NSS data show bathroom access and garbage collection gaps. When you design measures, **ask girls privately** about school toilets, disposal facilities and missed school days.
notes.88: Compare two surveys on shortage: 12.4% of rural households lacked sufficient water all year in 2018, and in 2022 43% of tap households faced a shortage at some time. Only 40% of those had any way to cope. Note the lesson in the last line: **plan visits for both the dry and the wet season**.
notes.89: Treat the NITI Aayog doubling figure as a projection and attribute it. It comes from 2008 demand estimates and assumptions about growth. The 2025 groundwater account, with 730 over-exploited units, is a measurement and weighs more in a district plan. The table shows three pressures: **irrigation, weather and contamination**.
notes.90: A pipe network is only as reliable as its source. Use the four questions as a design check: is the source a borewell in an over-exploited block, has its yield been measured in May, is there upstream recharge and a fallback. **Source sustainability is the adaptation measure a drinking water programme controls directly.**
notes.91: Work through three climate hazards for sanitation. Floods can release excreta from pits and tanks into lanes and shallow wells. Drought rations water, and 4.5% of rural latrine users reported no water in or around the latrine. Heat raises demand and shortens supply hours. Each design response **needs a named person** responsible for upkeep.
notes.92: Use the table as a pre-investment checklist covering drought, flood, heat, overextraction and saline intrusion. Each hazard names what fails and what to check. The slide says it turns the evidence of sections 6, 7 and 11 into questions you can answer in your first month. **Ask each question twice**, once for the dry season and once for the wet.
notes.94: Sort data into four kinds and keep each kind's typical error in mind. MIS data show what was built and miss use. A commissioned survey is run by the programme's own agency. National surveys are independent and infrequent. Trials are small. **Triangulate them, and disclose source, date, unit and collector** on every figure.
notes.95: Choose few indicators and define them in advance. Each row gives you the definition and the method, for example measured litres per person per day against the standard of 55, or last defecation for each person over two. The closing rule: **keep definitions fixed across rounds** so that change means change.
notes.96: Match each measurement method to its weakness. Self-report is cheap and inflated. Observation is expensive and changes behaviour. Spot checks, such as a wet pan or soap at the handwashing place, are harder to fake than a questionnaire. **Report the gap between them**, because the gap tells you how far reports can be trusted.
notes.97: Plan water quality monitoring as three layers. The 2022 assessment tested twelve parameters in labs and measured pH and chlorine on site. Field kits, used by village women, screen for common problems and should trigger a lab test. Remember that **a bacteriological test describes only the moment of sampling**, so repeat tests across seasons.
notes.98: Use the five-step plan as a template. Begin with a random panel of villages and households, ask each member about the last defecation, measure supply in May and October, test water at the source and the tap, and publish results next to the MIS figures. **Explain any gap** between the two.
notes.99: Use this slide as the reading list behind every figure in the course. It groups the sources into data and surveys, government statements, research and background. When you quote a number from the deck, go to its source and check the date. **Figures are current to October 2026.**
